recent_posts.title: The End Of Java's 1-Billion-Row Challenge (Ep. 5) | With @caseymuratori ​
recent_posts.summary: Final episode of a series tackling Java's 1-billion-row challenge, put on indefinite hold due to the host's promotion at JetBrains. The episode covers performance analysis methodology: establishing baselines, reading disassembly via JITWatch, and diagnosing why a simple newline-counting loop runs ~7x slower than a bare file read. Through buffer size experiments and loop stride tests, the hosts determine the bottleneck is instruction throughput rather than cache misses, concluding the JVM needs to emit a more efficient loop—ideally using SIMD/vectorization (Java's Vector API) to process 16 bytes at a time instead of byte-by-byte.

recent_posts.title: From Java to Assembly in Java's 1-Billion-Row Challenge (Ep. 4) | With @caseymuratori ​
recent_posts.summary: Episode 4 of a series tackling the 1-billion-row challenge in Java, focused on reading and understanding JVM-generated assembly code. The discussion covers how to extract assembly output from the JVM using the HotSpot disassembler, explains Java's tiered compilation pipeline (interpreter → C1 → C2), and uses Compiler Explorer (Godbolt) to demystify assembly by comparing a simple find-character loop in C against its Java JIT-compiled equivalent. Key takeaway: the JVM's C2 compiler produces roughly the same six-instruction loop as an optimized C compiler, but the surrounding overhead code raises questions about how much extra work runs per call when the function is invoked two billion times.

recent_posts.title: Slow For-Loops in Java's 1-Billion-Row Challenge (Ep. 3) | With @caseymuratori ​
recent_posts.summary: Episode 3 of solving the 1-billion-row challenge in Java, featuring a deep dive into performance analysis methodology. The hosts establish a baseline by reading a 13GB file from a RAM disk (~1.1 seconds), then add byte-by-byte scanning for semicolons and newlines, which unexpectedly jumps to ~11 seconds. They analyze why using CPU cycle math on an Apple M3 Max (4.05 GHz), concluding the JVM is likely generating inefficient loop code rather than the bottleneck being memory traffic. Discussion covers Java file I/O APIs (BufferedInputStream vs FileChannel vs memory-mapped files), ByteBuffer flip/clear semantics, CPU cache hierarchy (L1/L2 on Apple Silicon), optimal buffer sizing strategies, and the importance of inspecting JIT-compiled assembly output to verify what code is actually executing. Homework for next episode: set up JVM assembly inspection and test various buffer sizes.

recent_posts.title: Setting Performance Baselines for Java's 1-Billion-Row Challenge (Ep. 2) | With @caseymuratori
recent_posts.summary: A video episode exploring how to establish performance baselines for Java's 1-Billion-Row Challenge. The hosts discover the challenge runs from a RAM disk rather than an SSD, which explains sub-second results that seemed physically impossible. They benchmark SSD read speeds using the `dd` command (~6.5 GB/s cold), compare Java file-reading APIs (BufferedInputStream, FileChannel, MappedByteBuffer), and find FileChannel matches the raw DD baseline at ~2.1 seconds for a 15 GB file. The discussion covers OS file caching, PCIe lane bandwidth, disk block sizes, kernel privilege transitions, and why chunk sizes matter for throughput. Homework for next episode: implement a working solution and set up a RAM disk for testing.

recent_posts.title: Solving Java’s 1 Billion Row Challenge (Ep. 1) | With @caseymuratori
recent_posts.summary: First episode of a series dissecting a solution to the 1 Billion Row Challenge in Java, where a 13 GB text file with temperature measurements must be processed as fast as possible. The hosts walk through an initial approach using parallel file reading with memory-mapped files, splitting the file into chunks per thread, and parsing city names and temperature values. Key topics include hyperthreading vs physical cores, memory-mapped file unpredictability, the performance cost of Java's default string/double parsing, and the importance of establishing a hardware baseline (SSD read speed, file system cache behavior) before optimizing. Homework for the next episode: benchmark raw file read speed in Java against the SSD's theoretical peak throughput.

recent_posts.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) - Explained
recent_posts.summary: A practical introduction to Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's initiative for giving LLMs access to external data sources. Explains the architecture involving a host/client (e.g., Claude Desktop), an MCP server, and external data sources like GitHub. Walks through how the MCP server exposes a tools endpoint listing its capabilities, and how Claude orchestrates multiple requests to retrieve real data and summarize it. Demonstrates configuring Claude Desktop with the GitHub MCP server via a JSON config file, and shows the full request flow from user query to final LLM response.

recent_posts.title: Prompt Engineering - Basic Concepts For Developers
recent_posts.summary: A foundational guide to prompt engineering for developers building applications on top of LLMs. Covers how LLMs work as document completion engines, the ChatML format, context engineering (what to include and how to structure it), token limits, function calling for real-time data, stateful conversation loops, the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon, using structured formats like XML for parseable responses, and how to choose the right model based on cost, speed, and capability.

recent_posts.title: Building Docker Images - Best Practices
recent_posts.summary: A practical intermediate guide to optimizing Docker image builds for speed and size. Covers how every Dockerfile instruction creates a layer, why layers are additive (meaning deleted files still add to image size), and how to chain RUN commands to minimize layer bloat. Explains layer ordering rules: put rarely-changing, network-intensive steps at the top and frequently-changing files at the bottom to maximize cache hits. Also covers .dockerignore to reduce build context size, and Docker's mount cache flag for caching dependency directories (pip, npm, Maven) between builds to avoid re-downloading packages on every rebuild.
